title: である and the older copulas
summary: である is the plain, straight copula; だ and です are its short forms, and でございます is its polite version.

blocks.text: **である** is the copula in its full form. Historically だ is a short で + ある, and です is a short であります. You meet である in essays, news and textbooks, because it is neutral: neither casual (だ) nor polite (です).

The copula puts noun A inside the set named by noun B. The particle **で** draws a boundary ("within which") and **ある** means to exist, so で + ある means "exists within this boundary". Do not confuse the particle で with the て-form of the copula, which is also で.
The big use: before a noun
だ and です can only end a clause. Only a な-noun can modify a noun, with な. For any other noun, である is the one way to build a modifier:

blocks.jp: 医者である父は忙しい。
blocks.en: My father, who is a doctor, is busy.

blocks.text: 医者である父は忙しい。
Compare 医者の父 ("doctor father"), which is vaguer. And 丸のさま does not work, so we need である.

English uses "is" for both. Japanese keeps them apart: **copula** (これは猫だ, this belongs to the set "cat") versus **ある / いる** (庭に猫がいる, a cat exists there). Japanese teachers call the copula a kind of verb; this course keeps it as its own third engine, because it has its own て-form (で) and its own linking form (な).

items: だ = casual, です = polite, である = plain and written.
である can modify a noun; だ and です cannot.
The copula says "A belongs to set B"; ある says "A exists".

questions.instruction: What register is である?
questions.note: である is neither casual (だ) nor polite (です).

questions.instruction: Which form is very polite, used in shops and announcements?
questions.note: でございます is the very polite copula.

questions.note: だ and です only end a clause; である builds a modifier.

questions.note: だ cannot sit before a noun, but である can.
